title: Legionnaires' disease
wiki_lead:
Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila. Signs and symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, high fever, muscle pains, and headaches. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea may also occur. This often begins 2–10 days after exposure.
A legionellosis is any disease caused by Legionella, including Legionnaires' disease (a pneumonia) and Pontiac fever (a related upper respiratory tract infection), but Legionnaires' disease is the most common, so mentions of legionellosis often refer to Legionnaires' disease.
Legionella is found naturally in fresh water. It can contaminate hot water tanks, hot tubs, and cooling towers of large air conditioners. Typically, it is spread by breathing in mist that contains Legionella, and can also occur when contaminated water is aspirated. It typically does not spread directly between people, and most people who are exposed do not become infected. Risk factors for infection include older age, a history of smoking, chronic lung disease, and poor immune function. Those with severe pneumonia and those with pneumonia and a recent travel history should be tested for the disease. Diagnosis is by a urinary antigen test and sputum culture.
No vaccine is available. Prevention depends on good maintenance of water systems. Treatment of Legionnaires' disease is commonly conducted with antibiotics. Recommended agents include the fluoroquinolones levofloxacin and moxifloxacin, and the macrolide azithromycin. Hospitalization is often required. The fatality rate is around 10% for previously healthy people, but up to 25% in those with underlying conditions.
The numbers of cases that occur globally is not known. Legionnaires' disease is the cause of an estimated 2–9% of pneumonia cases that are acquired outside of a hospital. An estimated 8,000 to 18,000 cases a year in the United States require hospitalization. Outbreaks of disease account for a minority of cases. While it can occur any time of the year, it is more common in the summer and autumn. The disease is named after the outbreak where it was first identified, at a 1976 American Legion convention in Philadelphia.

The length of time between exposure to the bacteria and the appearance of symptoms (incubation period) is generally 2–10 days, but more rarely can extend to as long as 20 days. For the general population, among those exposed, between 0.1 and 5.0% develop the disease, while among those in hospital, between 0.4 and 14% develop the disease.
Those with Legionnaires' disease usually have fever, chills, and a cough, which may be dry or may produce sputum. Almost all experience fever, while around half have cough with sputum, and one-third cough up blood or bloody sputum. grok_lead: Legionnaires' disease is a severe form of pneumonia resulting from infection by Legionella bacteria, predominantly Legionella pneumophila. The infection occurs through inhalation of fine water droplets aerosolized from contaminated man-made water systems, such as cooling towers, hot tubs, and plumbing fixtures, rather than direct person-to-person transmission. Symptoms typically include high fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, and muscle aches, progressing rapidly in susceptible individuals to respiratory failure or multi-organ involvement if untreated. The disease derives its name from a 1976 outbreak in Philadelphia, where 182 cases emerged among attendees of an American Legion convention, resulting in 29 deaths and prompting the identification of the causative pathogen after extensive investigation. This event marked the first recognized epidemic of the illness, though retrospective analyses indicate sporadic cases predated it. Risk factors for severe outcomes include advanced age, smoking, chronic lung conditions, immunosuppression, and recent heavy alcohol use, with healthy individuals often exposed asymptomatically or developing milder Pontiac fever, a non-pneumonic flu-like syndrome caused by the same bacteria. Effective antibiotics like macrolides or fluoroquinolones, combined with supportive care, yield high recovery rates when initiated promptly, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis via urinary antigen testing or culture. Incidence has risen in recent decades due to improved surveillance and aging populations, with prevention centered on water system maintenance to limit bacterial amplification in warm, stagnant environments.
